analysis.title: Strategist's Corner: The Last Customer Is the Most Profitable, But the Next One May Reset the Cost Curve
key_insights: Author Robert Almeida (MFS Global Investment Strategist) argues that in Internet 2.0 the last customer served by an established platform was the most profitable, because fixed costs were already absorbed and serving a new user cost little.

Internet 2.0 economics rested on falling capital intensity and muted competition. The author says investors treated them as normal, reinforced by passive investing, when they belonged to a unique capital cycle.

AI reverses this. Companies are directing more capital into datacenters, power systems, semiconductors, factories and supply chains, while AI lowers the cost of trying new things and draws more challengers into profit pools.

The existing platform's last customer may stay highly profitable. The next customer may require a larger capital base, since once capacity fills, more demand may need another datacenter, power commitment or production line.

The next customer brings three added costs. Cost to win: more competitors but not more hours in the day, so attention requires more content and marketing. Cost to serve: AI services need more infrastructure as usage rises, running on expensive power, memory and compute. Cost to keep: specialists can reach customers without rebuilding an incumbent's organization, so the leader may spend more with less pricing power.
An incumbent's economics can weaken without the business disappearing, if it earns a lower return on the next dollar.
Illustration: $10 earned on $100 of capital is a 10% return. Earning the same $10 on $200 of capital is 5%. Accounting profit is unchanged but the economics are not, and this matters to stock prices.

Compounders and cyclicals are distinguished by how returns behave as capital and competition respond, not by sector. A cyclical can look like a compounder in periods of scarcity, but high returns attract capital and competition and may extend a cycle rather than compound value.

The author defines quality as the ability to reinvest profitably through a full cycle, not high margins today. The market may reward the fastest grower in a boom, but long-term investors earn the full-cycle return.

Three tests for investors: does the business earn above its cost of capital today, can it reinvest the next dollar at an attractive return, and can it keep its gains after customers and competitors respond.

The author concludes the prior cycle rewarded exposure to established profit pools, while the emerging cycle should reward selectivity. A benchmark owns companies at today's weights, and fundamental investors can assess whether the next dollar of growth creates value before the index adjusts. The piece argues against abandoning active management.
risk_factors: Rising capital intensity from AI buildout (datacenters, power, semiconductors) may lower returns on the next dollar of revenue.
More challengers entering profit pools as AI lowers the cost of trying new things may weaken incumbents' pricing power.
Cyclical businesses can look like compounders during scarcity, and the bust math applies if capacity grows as pricing power weakens.

key_data_points.figure: 10% return on $100 of capital vs 5% return on $200 of capital
key_data_points.metric: Illustrative return on capital for the same $10 of profit
key_data_points.context: Hypothetical example showing that unchanged accounting profit can carry lower economic returns when more capital is required
key_data_points.anchor: Suppose a company earns $10 on $100 of capital: a 10% return. If earning the same $10 required $200, the return would fall to 5%.

key_data_points.metric: Author's tenure at MFS, cited as the source of the 'last customer is the most profitable' axiom
key_data_points.context: Background on the author, not a market figure
key_data_points.anchor: In my 27 years at MFS, one axiom has stood out in the Investment Department

tension_points.theme: AI capital intensity and incumbent returns
tension_points.bull_case: The last customer served by an existing platform may remain extraordinarily profitable because the investment has already been made, and a true compounder reinvests at attractive returns across a full cycle.
tension_points.bear_case: The next customer may require a larger capital base, more marketing, better service or a lower price, so the incumbent may earn a lower return on the next dollar even if accounting profit is unchanged.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A business that earns above its cost of capital today, can reinvest the next dollar at an attractive return, and keeps its gains after customers and competitors respond passes the author's three tests.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI raises the capital needed to win, serve and keep the next customer, so selectivity matters more than owning established profit pools.
theme_stances.evidence: The emerging cycle should reward selectivity.

theme_stances.key_argument: Investors abandoning active management today may be giving up on selectivity just as it begins to matter more.
theme_stances.evidence: giving up on selectivity just as it begins to matter more

contextual_mentions: AI datacenter, power and semiconductor capital spending raising capital intensity
AI lowering barriers and drawing challengers into incumbent profit pools
Internet 2.0 low marginal cost of serving the last customer
Cost to win, serve and keep the next customer
Compounders versus cyclicals by returns on incremental capital
Passive investing reinforcing Internet 2.0 margin assumptions
Quality defined as full-cycle reinvestment ability, not current margins
Active management case based on selectivity versus benchmark weights
